 Live Updates: Democrat Roy Cooper flips key Senate seat in North Carolina
 Politics 
 Updated on Nov 3, 2026 8:55 PM EST — Published on
 Nov 3, 2026 11:00 AM EST
 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check 
 Voters across the country are deciding control of the U.S. House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Polls have closed in 11 states, and results are beginning to roll into AP's election system.
 WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage 
 Power in Congress would give Democrats a means of rebuffing President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins. All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.
 Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News 
 Voters say the economy and the state of democracy are the top issues facing the country, with high costs and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds, according to the AP Voter Poll. The poll points to a midterm electorate that is deeply unhappy with the country's direction and pessimistic about the future.
 Here's the latest.
 8:55 p.m. EST
 JB Pritzker says his reelection as Illinois governor shows hope is winning out over fear
 "It looks like maybe, just maybe, something is stirring in the conscience of America," Pritzker told his supporters after winning election to a third term. He's the first Democrat elected to a third term as governor in Illinois.
 Pritzker is considered a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028.
 "We climbed one mountain tonight," Pritzker said. "But we are sitting at the base of another."
 Pritzker defeated Republican Darren Bailey, a former state lawmaker.
 Mike Collins says result not 'what we wanted'
 The Republican acknowledged the result in the Georgia Senate race in a brief speech to his supporters.
 "The results may not be what we wanted tonight, but y'all, that's OK. I'm going to continue to serve," he said.
 Collins, a current House member, praised Trump, calling it an honor and privilege to serve under him.
 Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won the seat.
 8:47 p.m. EST
 Cooper supporters cheer former governor's Senate win
 Supporters erupted into cheers, hugs and chants when they learned the former governor had won election to the U.S. Senate representing North Carolina.
 A crowd gathered in a downtown Raleigh hotel ballroom Tuesday night, where music was thumping and CNN played on a big screen. When the news of Cooper's victory appeared, the crowd exploded and began chanting, "Cooper! Cooper!"
 LIVE RESULTS: Roy Cooper wins Senate race in North Carolina 
 Anderson Clayton, who leads North Carolina's Democratic Party, said Cooper's decades in elected office made him an especially strong candidate.
 "He's woven into the fabric of North Carolina," she said.
 By electing Cooper, North Carolina voters chose "competence over chaos," Democratic Gov. Josh Stein said in a speech shortly after the race was called.
 Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley.
 Sununu says 'it's not our night'
 The Republican says he had a great message and vision but came up short in his New Hampshire Senate race against Democrat Chris Pappas.
 "This has been an incredible campaign, but it is not our night. I called Chris to congratulate him a few minutes ago. He ran a good race. More importantly, we ran a good race," John E. Sununu told supporters.
 Pappas, who is in his fourth term in the U.S. House, will replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a three-term Democrat who ousted Sununu in 2008.
 Pappas says 'New Hampshire showed up today'
 Pappas says his U.S. Senate victory in New Hampshire is proof that Washington needs a "new generation at the table to fix things."
 "This has been a long campaign against the backdrop of chaos, corruption and costs coming out of Washington," Pappas told supporters in Manchester. "New Hampshire showed up today, you spoke up today, you said in a resounding voice that New Hampshire needs a course correction. Washington needs a new generation at the table to fix things."
 8:38 p.m. EST
 Pappas' win blocks a path for GOP Senate gains
 Democrat Chris Pappas in New Hampshire has blocked an opportunity for Republicans to gain a seat as they try to hold onto their Senate majority.
 Pappas, a four-term House member, had called his Republican opponent John Sununu, a former U.S. senator, "the wrong Sununu" in a reference to the popular former Republican Gov. Chris Sununu. Republicans thought the race could work as a check against potential Democratic gains.
 LIVE RESULTS: Chris Pappas wins Senate race in New Hampshire 
 With New Hampshire and Georgia staying in Democratic hands, Republicans now look to Michigan for a pickup, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is competing with Republican Mike Rogers.
 Pappas is also the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate.
 Juliana Stratton makes history with Black women in the Senate
 Illinois Democrat Stratton's election marks the first time in history three Black women will be in office at the same time in the U.S. Senate. She'll join two other Black Democratic women — Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, who were not up this election cycle.
 Sen. Jon Ossoff supporters erupt in cheers
 Ossoff's supporters who'd gathered Tuesday night at a downtown Atlanta hotel erupted in cheers, hugged and kissed when television screens around the room showed Ossoff had won.
 Ossoff is expected to address the crowd later in the evening.
 Many of the supporters said Ossoff represented an important generational shift for their party.
 "He's bringing in a lot of young voters and that is what we need right now to get the young voters on the right way of life, showing them which way to go," said Jennifer Gray, 63, a retired IRS employee. "Ossoff, he talks to them. And because he's younger, they're listening to him."
 8:15 p.m. EST
 Republicans once saw Georgia seat as within reach, until Ossoff surged
 Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff's reelection blocks a targeted effort by Republicans to pick up a Senate seat.
 The Democrat's victory over Republican Mike Collins is a notable turnabout from last year, when Republicans were optimistic about the state, given that Trump carried it narrowly in the 2024 presidential race.
 LIVE RESULTS: Jon Ossoff wins Senate reelection in Georgia 
 Instead, Ossoff dominated in fundraising throughout the campaign. Republican groups supporting Collins pulled back their spending in mid-October, signaling the race was likely lost.
 Democrats' hope of gaining the majority is premised on holding seats in Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
 What to watch for after polls close at 8 p.m. ET
 The 8 p.m. hour is primetime on election night, with polls fully or partially closing in almost half the states, including key states like Florida, Maine, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.
 Florida tends to have one of the faster counts in this time slot, since results in most of the state start releasing in the 7 p.m. hour. In 2024, the Florida vote count was 90% complete by 8:07 p.m.
 READ MORE: Here's when polls are closing in each state this midterm election 
 The 2024 vote counts in New Hampshire and Pennsylvania reached the halfway mark at 10:12 p.m. They reached 90% at 12:48 a.m. in Pennsylvania and 1:42 a.m. in New Hampshire. Maine didn't reach the halfway mark in 2024 until 12:54 a.m.
 Polls in almost all of Michigan and Texas close at 8 p.m., including in the states' most competitive congressional districts, but no statewide winners will be declared until the final polls have closed at 9 p.m.
 Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Florida, Maine and New Hampshire; gubernatorial races in Florida and Pennsylvania; and U.S. House races in Alabama, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas.
 7:53 p.m. EST
 Black voter turnout appears robust on Election Day, voter coalition says
 LaTosha Brown, co-founder of the voting rights group Black Voters Matter, said turnout in some states seemed to rival that of 2008, when Democrat Barack Obama was running for president for the first time.
 She and others said turnout appeared particularly high in Michigan and Mississippi.
 A supporter looks on outside the venue for the Election Night rally of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during the US midterm elections in Detroit, Michigan, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Dieu-Nalio Chery/Reuters
 Brown, speaking during a media briefing organized by the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, said her organization had more than 2,000 poll observers in several states. They reported no "widescale issues" for voters, she said.
 Melanie Campbell, president and CEO of the coalition, said the group has extended its monitoring efforts beyond Election Day — through vote counting, certifications and even winners' inaugurations.
 "As those of us who believe that this democracy is for all people, we have to also stand in the gap," she said.
 7:33 p.m. EST
 Civil rights group says ICE social media message intended to intimidate voters
 Carmen Feliciano, vice president for policy and advocacy at the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS, criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for a social media post that said, in part: "If you vote illegally, we will find you."
 The agency posted the message on Election Day.
 "This is part of a strategy we have been seeing for the last few years — intimidation and trying to block people from going out to the polls," Feliciano said.
 She noted that Latino turnout was expected to be high for the midterm elections.
 Asked why the message went out, the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, issued a statement that read in part: "ONLY Americans should elect American leaders."
 Throughout the day, ICE announced arrests or charges against people suspected of voting as noncitizens in previous elections.
 7:14 p.m. EST
 Key U.S. House races to watch in Florida
 A handful of key U.S. House races in Florida could offer early signs of how Democrats are performing tonight.
 LIVE RESULTS: Florida Senate midterm election 
 Democratic Reps. Darren Soto and Kathy Castor are defending their seats in the redrawn 9th and 14th Districts. Both of the districts would have favored Trump by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election.
 The 22nd District is an open seat after Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel opted to run in the 23rd District when her district was redrawn.
 What to watch for after polls close at 7 p.m. ET
 All polls close at 7 p.m. in six states, including Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia, which tend to complete almost all of their vote counting on election night.
 In the 2024 general election, the vote count in all three states reached the halfway mark in the 8 p.m. hour. The counts were 90% complete at 10:21 p.m. in Georgia, 11:14 p.m. in South Carolina and 12:07 a.m. in Virginia. In Georgia's competitive presidential contest, The Associated Press declared Trump the winner at 12:58 a.m.
 Democratic and Republican observers review ballots during midterm elections at the Fulton County Election Hub and Operation Center in Fairburn, Georgia, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Edgar Su/Reuters
 Most Florida polls will also close at 7 p.m., including in every competitive congressional district, but no statewide winners will be declared until polls in the Central Time Zone close at 8 p.m.
 Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia close at 7:30 p.m. All three states also count votes relatively quickly, reaching the halfway point at around 9 p.m. in 2024 and about 90% in the 11 p.m. hour. The AP declared a winner in Ohio's competitive 2024 U.S. Senate race at 11:27 p.m.
 Some key contests to watch in this hour are U.S. Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio; gubernatorial races in Georgia and Ohio; and U.S. House races in Florida, Indiana, South Carolina, Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.
 6:52 p.m. EST
 Flooding strands voters on the Navajo Nation
 Hundreds of voters in Rock Point, Arizona, on the Navajo Nation were unable to reach the polls Tuesday as flooding had closed a major bridge and washed out dirt roads, a tribal official said.
 On a typical Election Day, the chapter house parking lot would be buzzing with voters, candidates and pop-up food stalls.
 "Unfortunately, today that parking lot is underwater," said Valinda Shirley, vice president of the Rock Point Chapter, the local seat of tribal government.
 Officials moved the polling place across the street to an administration building, but many residents remained stranded.
 "I have people that are still texting me asking how I can get them out so they can vote," Shirley said Tuesday afternoon.
 The flooding is keeping those residents from casting ballots in both the U.S. midterms and races for Navajo Nation president and council delegates.
 6:38 p.m. EST
 Jeffries says House Democrats are ready to deliver the 'best version' of America
 Jeffries, who's in line to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if Democrats seize control and elect him to the job, said House Democrats don't work for any president.
 "We work for all of you, the American people, and we're committed to delivering an America that's the best version of herself," he said.
 He told the volunteers that Democrats are "committed to ending this national nightmare, fighting to make this country affordable" and "continuing our country's long, necessary and majestic march toward a more perfect union."
 He urged them on: "Let's go win this thing."
 6:11 p.m. EST
 Jeffries says Democrats 'on the brink' of taking back the House
 House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries popped by to rally and thank volunteers at a phone bank in Washington for battleground House candidates.
 "We're on the brink of a dramatic change in the direction in the country," Jeffries said.
 "We're on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives."
 He said a Democratic win would be a victory for Americans.
 "We're going to deliver a Congress that actually puts the American people first," he said.
 Volunteers applaud as House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries gives two thumbs at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) midterm election night phone bank and watch party at a hotel in Washington, D.C., Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters
 Democrats are dialing voters in an election evening push for the House
 House Democrats have opened a phone bank in Washington with dozens of volunteers calling voters in key House races across the country before polls close.
 They're encouraging voters to cast ballots as Democrats work to wrest control of the House from Republicans.
 5:57 p.m. EST
 Ballot shortages cause delays at some Chicago voting sites
 Some Chicago polling places ran out of paper ballots.
 Chicago Board of Elections spokesperson Julie Metea said more ballots would be printed and that everyone in line by the time polls close would be able to vote — though it might be a long wait for an electronic voting machine. Voters could also go to one of the city's universal voting centers.
 In the Logan Square neighborhood, Jenna Roggensack, 37, said poll workers told her in the morning to return later. Because she's a teacher who had the day off, that was possible — if inconvenient. When she returned, she said she had to wait an hour and a half, though ultimately did get to vote.
 Later in the afternoon, though, a poll worker emerged and told those waiting outside that they had run out of paper ballots again.
 5:36 p.m. EST
 House races to watch: Districts that flipped in 2024
 The handful of House members who flipped the toughest seats in 2024 all face challenging races again this year. Can they avoid a sophomore slump?
 WATCH: Mapping the battle for control of the House 
 Most of these districts flipped to the GOP in 2024, riding Trump's coattails as he clinched a second term. The good news for these Republicans is that it's almost always easier to win a seat that you already represent. The bad news is that many of them won their seats by tiny margins and are facing a much tougher national environment this time around.
 DOJ escalates criminal investigation of Alaska Senate candidate
 The Trump administration notified prominent Democratic attorney Marc Elias and others that they may be targets of the inquiry, which focuses on a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
 That's according to two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
 READ MORE: FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's hometown as Alaska Senate inquiry widens 
 Trump's DOJ is investigating retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for Senate, which the president says will confuse voters because he shares a first and last name with Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. The New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
 "This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets," Elias said in a statement Tuesday.
 Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, Republican candidate for reelection, accompanied by his wife Julie Fate Sullivan, arrives to vote during the midterm elections, in Anchorage, Alaska, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Emily Mesner/Reuters
 4:41 p.m. EST
 Immigration enforcement agency issues warning to voters
 Federal immigration officials took to social media on Election Day to warn against illegal voting by noncitizens.
 In a message on X, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote: "If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape."
 The agency did not return messages seeking comment about the post. Throughout Tuesday, it also posted about arrests of noncitizens accused of voting.
 While that has been a major emphasis for the agency this year, the number of arrests and earlier investigations in the states demonstrate the problem is rare.
 READ MORE: Justice Department urges sanctions for database analysis critical of its noncitizen voting claims 
 David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the post unfortunate but said heavy early voting suggested the administration's tactics appeared to have no effect on turnout.
 "If there were individuals in this administration who thought that they could scare voters away from this election, they're going to be disappointed," he said.
 Incumbents in redrawn districts face very different electorates than in 2024
 Many incumbents running for reelection in redrawn districts are facing a very different set of voters than they currently represent.
 Several districts went from being majority-nonwhite to majority-white after mid-decade redistricting. These are also some of the places that shifted the most toward Trump when comparing the 2024 vote margin under old and new congressional boundaries.
 Similarly, a number of districts shifted from being majority-white to being majority-nonwhite. Many of these districts also shifted toward Harris, but some in Texas and Florida moved further to the right.
 4:16 p.m. EST
 Michigan raised concerns about federal monitors in two cities
 Michigan election officials objected after hearing that federal poll monitors in Dearborn and Flint were asking workers about their training or requesting to see training materials, a spokesperson said.
 "This is not permitted under the law," said Angela Benander of the Department of State.
 The U.S. Justice Department agreed and pledged to inform the election monitors, Benander said.
 Separately, she said federal monitors in Lansing were trying to talk to voters, which is OK if the exchange happens after a ballot is cast and is outside the polling place.
 "We don't have any concerns," Benander said.
 People vote during the midterm elections at a polling site in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Dieu-Nalio Chery/Reuters
 4:11 p.m. EST
 3 precincts in Pennsylvania extend voting hours due to machine issues
 Officials in Pennsylvania's Chester County say they're extending voting hours in three precincts after "machine set-up issues" delayed the opening of polling sites just west of Philadelphia.
 The Chester County Court of Common Pleas granted the three precincts a 30-minute extension, meaning voters will be able to cast ballots until 8:30 p.m. EST, according to the county.
 Voters casting ballots at these three sites after 8 p.m. EST — when polling stations close statewide — will use provisional ballots.
 5 polling sites will stay open late in North Carolina
 Election officials extended voting hours at each location after county election supervisors reported delays caused by technical problems with computers.
 The longest extension granted by the North Carolina State Board of Elections was 45 minutes at one location in Columbus County, where officials said computer problems forced election workers to switch to backup paper poll books, slowing lines Tuesday morning.
 Two precincts in Hertford County and one each in Lenoir and Wilson counties also will stay open an extra 15 to 30 minutes. The five-member board approved each extension unanimously.
 The extended hours mean state election officials in North Carolina won't begin reporting results until after the last polling site closes at 8:15 p.m. ET, said Adam Steele, an attorney for the election board. He said county election officials will tally their votes without delay.
 Polls in North Carolina close at 7:30 p.m. ET, unless extended by the board.
 Latest views on the 2 major parties from AP-NORC polling
 At least half of U.S. adults have a negative opinion of the two parties, according to AP-NORC polling.
 About half have a "very" or "somewhat" unfavorable view of the Democratic Party in an AP-NORC poll from October, while just over half say that about the Republican Party.
 Roughly 7 in 10 Democrats hold a favorable view of their own party, which is down from 85% in September 2024. Republicans, however, feel about as positively as they did two years ago, with 85% in the latest polling saying they have a favorable view of the Republican Party.
 Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults feel "very" or "somewhat" optimistic about the future of the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. Republicans are a bit more optimistic about their party's future than Democrats are — slightly fewer than half of Republicans, 46%, say they are feeling positive, compared to 35% of Democrats.
 3:58 p.m. EST
 In Texas, Korean vet voter weighs in on Iran war
 In southeastern Texas, Juventino Sáenz accompanied a relative to the polls in McAllen.
 The 91-year-old Korean War veteran who said he'd voted early shared his feelings about Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.
 Sáenz blamed Iran but also blamed Trump, saying the president should have gone to Congress for permission.
 "He couldn't do it just because he's the president," Sáenz said.
 He said he's backed Republicans in the past, citing his votes for Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush for president.
 But in the closely watched Texas U.S. Senate race, Sáenz said he voted for Talarico, the Democrat, because he didn't like Paxton's record or that Paxton's own Republican Party impeached him.
 "He was doing a lot of things that were not right," he said of Paxton.
 Pain at the pump powers voter fury
 Gas prices have shot up by nearly a third since Trump launched his war against Iran, fueling voter distress about the economy and high prices. But another fuel source has risen even higher and caused potentially more pain.
 That's diesel fuel, which powers not just a whole bunch of farming and industrial equipment but the ships and trucks that transport a range of goods and services to voters' doors.
 READ MORE: Trump administration promised farmers $15 billion in weeks before midterms 
 Diesel prices have nearly doubled since the start of the Iran war. A disproportionate share of the oil that comes through the Strait of Hormuz is used to make diesel. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries that produce the fuel added to the shortage.
 That pushed Trump to take controversial action to try to lower the price of diesel, cutting a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel from his country to the U.S. But even that hasn't significantly brought diesel prices down.
 3:38 p.m. EST
 Ranks of Black governors could grow with 8 nominees nationwide
 Maryland's Wes Moore is the only Black governor in the U.S., and he's only the third elected Black governor in history, all of them Democrats and men.
 But Moore, who's heavily favored for reelection, could soon have company.
 There are seven additional Black major party nominees for governor. They include Republicans and Democrats, men and women. Each would be the first Black chief executive in their respective states.
 Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor and a Democrat, and Minnesota's Lisa Demuth, a former state legislative leader and a Republican, could each make history. No Black woman has ever been elected as governor.
 LIVE RESULTS: Georgia governor midterm election 
 Two Black Republican men are on gubernatorial ballots: Byron Donalds in Florida and John James in Michigan. Both are U.S. representatives currently.
 Three other Black men, all Democrats, round out the slate: Aaron Ford in Nevada, Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina and David Crowley in Wisconsin.
 Early vote count reaches nearly 60 million as Election Day voting continues
 More than 59 million people have voted so far, according to an Associated Press analysis.
 The advance vote has spiked ahead of Election Day compared to 2022. There were 59.7 million ballots cast as of Tuesday, compared to a little over 58 million in 2022.
 The tally includes early in-person and mail balloting.
 The election will determine which party controls the House and Senate.
 A Trump-backed redistricting plan goes to voters
 At Trump's urging, Republicans in eight states adopted new congressional districts to try to gain an edge in the midterm elections. But after a long legal battle, Missouri's new map was blocked by both the U.S. Supreme Court and the Missouri Supreme Court because of a referendum petition.
 Voters are now deciding whether to uphold or reject the new map. If approved, it could be used in the 2028 election.
 Maryland voters are deciding a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for a new House map in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents have urged a "yes" vote as a means to "stop Trump."
 READ MORE: About 35 million people have been put into new House districts in the fight over congressional maps, report says 
 Some Colorado Democrats also want to redistrict. But a citizen initiative on the ballot there would prohibit any potential redistricting for 2028 from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
 Some voters in Georgia receive false texts from an unknown sender about polling site changes
 A few hiccups have come up in Fulton County, Georgia, a Democratic stronghold Trump has long falsely accused of widespread voter fraud that he says caused him to lose the state in 2020.
 Some voters have reported receiving texts that were not sent by the county about polling place changes, according to Fulton County's Facebook page. A county spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
 Kyle Gomez-Leineweber, policy director at election watchdog group Common Cause Georgia, said the group was aware of the texts but didn't know who sent them or if they were based on incorrect information or were intentionally trying to mislead voters.
 Gomez-Leineweber said volunteers have been telling people to double-check information with official sources.
 Separately, about 1,000 ballots received during early voting last month will be rescanned "as a precaution" due to equipment failures with two scanners, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said Tuesday. He said it would not delay election results.
 Progressive Democrats try flipping swing House districts
 Election workers extract mail-in ballots for the midterm election at the Registrar of Voters in San Diego, California, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/ Reuters
 Democrats' path to winning the House could rest with progressive candidates challenging Republicans in districts that swung between Trump and Joe Biden.
 In California's 22nd District, incumbent Rep. David Valadao faces Democratic challenger Randy Villegas, who has Sen. Bernie Sanders' endorsement.
 In Colorado's 8th District, Rep. Gabe Evans faces Democrat Manny Rutinel, who had campaigned with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
 In Michigan's 7th District, Rep. Tom Barrett is up against Will Lawrence, a longtime liberal activist and former member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
 Republicans are hoping their rivals' political backgrounds are a mismatch in districts that are by and large evenly divided politically.
 2:59 p.m. EST
 3 NASA astronauts cast ballots from the space station
 Astronaut Anil Menon's sleeping compartment aboard the International Space Station doubled as his voting booth. Menon said in a brief video posted via X on Tuesday that he used his computer to fill out and submit an electronic ballot to Harris County, Texas. Crewmates Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney did the same.
 Harris County is home to NASA's Johnson Space Center and Mission Control.
 U.S. astronauts have been voting in space since 1997.
 Values motivate Texas voters — but for different candidates
 In the Dallas suburbs, two voters say Christian values factored into their votes.
 James Bender said he wants the country to get back to an identity rooted in Judeo-Christian values.
 He said he respected Talarico's religious roots and faith but said, "At the end of the day, I just, I don't agree with him."
 Bender, 47, said he wasn't voting for Paxton's character as much as the policies he'd try to enact if elected.
 Paxton has faced a string of legal and ethical problems and allegations of marital infidelity.
 April Vindiola said those issues made Paxton a "no" for her. She said a candidate's morals and values are important.
 "I've been following Talarico for quite some time," Vindiola said. "I think whenever I've heard him speak … it resonates with me what his beliefs are."
 Republican governor hopeful to voters in liberal California: 'Just try it!'
 The last time California elected a Republican to statewide office, George W. Bush was president, entertainer James Brown was still alive and the second "Pirates of the Caribbean" movie was the biggest film of the year.
 Republican Steve Hilton is trying to defy those odds and end his party's 16-year drought in a state with 4.5 million more registered Democratic voters than Republicans.
 He's tried to win over Californians who rarely vote Republican by repeating the motto "Just try it!"; blaming Democratic leadership for the state's high cost of living; and releasing splashy ads, sometimes using AI to mock his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra.
 Becerra, meanwhile, has campaigned on a promise to uphold the state's status as a liberal counterweight to Trump's policies. He's tried to tie Hilton to Trump, who endorsed him in the primary.
 California billionaire tax proposal tests voters' appetite to 'tax the rich'
 A cigarette butt is placed on an "I voted" sign during the midterm elections on Skid Row in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Evelyn Hockstein/ Reuters
 The ballot measure, known as Proposition 40, has racked up support from progressives like Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who has framed it as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality, while also drawing criticism from Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democrats, who say it will trigger wealthy people to flee the state.
 The ballot fight has also been defined by the copious amount of money tech moguls and venture capitalists have poured into it. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has donated more than $100 million to a political committee working to defeat the proposal.
 The first-in-the-nation measure would levy a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would be used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, while 10% would go toward education and food assistance programs.
 In Virginia, a retiree says Trump has 'done a great job'
 Joni Borrell, 67, and her father, Herman Jamerson, 91, described themselves as solidly Republican. They voted that way a week before Election Day, casting ballots in Henrico, Virginia, for GOP Rep. Rob Wittman and Bert Mizusawa, the Republican mounting a long-shot bid against Democratic incumbent Sen. Mark Warner.
 Jamerson, a retired plumbing contractor, said he thinks the president has "done a great job" so far this term.
 "He's for the common person. To me, that's his biggest success. I mean, he looks out for the little guy, just the average person," Jamerson said.
